projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Chester Michael Matyjasik was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Chester Matyjasik. Mr. Matyjasik served in the U.S. Army with Battery B of the 254th Field Artillery Battalion. Chester's highest rank was First Sergeant and he served in the European Theater. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Matyjasik's home in Mentor, Ohio, on June 3, 2003. Chester was 80 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: In 1941 I was living in the town I was born in, Mogadore, Ohio. Proud of it, very small town. Reminds me of a town out west. They had a sheriff there, one grocery store, one butcher shop, the hotel is still there, the caboose is still there, barber shop is still there, and I go there quite often. I went to my school that I didn't go to since 1936 and they was all surprised when I told them how much of a change it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you say you just turned 80 recently?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: I turned 80 February the 24th. I was born in 1923.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you would have been 18 in 1941. Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: I remember the 7th, yes. Yes, I remember that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What do you remember about the attack on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, actually I thought that was a horrible thing because I think the set up wasn't actually looked forward to as the way it should have been. I can remember where the one guard or whatever he was, a radio man, actually knew there was trouble and tried to get ahold of people but then I think they was actually -- it was on a weekend and to me it sounded like it was because they was actually having, you know, their party or whatever, celebrating. They had everything all ready, but they didn't do what they had to do. And when he did call in they thought it was actually a joke. Well, I suppose if I had been in their shoes I'd have probably thought the same thing on account of one thing, we never thought that could ever happen in America to us. It actually caught us sleeping. And we were all dressed up. I wished they were in boots because there was water. We lost so many there and actually that could have been the start of the war and the end of the war if they'd have finished it right there, I think Japanese. So we were very fortunate, though, they did get some of the stuff down from Japan. I think they even got some of their torpedoes -- I mean their submarines and stuff like that, but they didn't get enough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, I'm sad about that because, just like I say, America should not fall asleep. We've got to be on alert all the time. Best country in the world, and everybody knows it, and I don't know but people without greed are happy that America is where it is because we help everybody. We don't stop at nobody.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you out of school at that time?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Yes, I was. I was out of school, yes. I was working on the AC&Y Railroad, I was a fireman promoted engineer on the railroad, and that's in Akron, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, would that job have meant that you -- would that have meant that you had a deferment from the draft?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Yes, I did have a deferment. When I came back -- all I had to go was go back. I came back and I only stayed out of work for a week. I had my fun for one week with my dad alone, we went all over, and I could even say I had a couple of drinks to celebrate with my dad. We got along fine. And I can tell you a story about my father and a flag. He was from Poland and actually came to America. Now, when I was a boy, and say at the age of three, my dad had one flag in the house and he always says, This is the best flag that I ever saw. He got his citizenship papers after he had the flag, even. And very proud of it. And actually I don't know what happened to the flag but I had it for years and years but when somebody finds out stuff like that they actually take it away from you and it hurts but then I'm glad they still got it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, were you eventually drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: I got -- I enlisted. I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About when was that?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: In the early part of '43. I think it was something like January of '43, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you probably didn't have to enlist, right? You would have been probably not drafted because of your job?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, actually, I wouldn't have been drafted if I didn't want to because I actually signed up for the Navy, but the day before I was supposed to go to Norfolk my friend and I went for a ride -- because I had a nice car then -- and I got hurt. And I went in the hospital for 17 days. And they had the shore patrols around our house for 17 days but they never checked nothing about that. They didn't check. But when I got out -- it was a country home. I had to walk down a railroad track -- I walked a mile as soon as I got out of the hospital. I had 47 stitches and eight clamps on my body. I was hurt pretty bad. They gave me a 50-50 chance and ten days to live. But, anyway, when they saw that I was coming down the road they all come down, and -- my dad, of course, you know, from Poland, why they did knock on the door -- and our doors were open 24 hours a day. It didn't make no difference. Anybody that wanted to come in they could come in or go when they pleased. And what happened, then, they started to grab me and my dad went in for a shotgun, it didn't look good, but anyhow, he did. So turn around and they had to call -- we had a sheriff, you could have called him a marshal, that's how small the town was. So then he went up -- they got the marshal and they told him, Okay, settle it, because he says, You didn't have to do what you did to grab the boy, all you had to do was ask. So then I waited, I think, about two months and I went back to the Navy and they would not accept me because I still wasn't healed up properly. I volunteered for the Army and the doctor that actually operated on me and that was a doctor that says, You don't have to go, but I says, I might just as well go now, because, I says, I'll have to go anyhow. So I did. And I'm happy I did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where did you train, then?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: I trained in Camp Gordon, Georgia.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: My training was pretty good. Actually when we first got in it was a little rough, but I was never a homesick boy due to the fact that I was in the civilian reserve corps when I was 15 years old but you wasn't allowed to get in until you was 16 but we fixed up my birth certificate. I'm telling you this now because -- but it was really funny. As soon as you got your reenlistment signed for the three C's then you just tear up your birth certificate. It only cost 50 cents so it wasn't too bad. So then I was in the three C's for a year, and then I was the civilian reserve corps for about seven and a half years, but the Army, they took me in. And just like I say, the training I got at Camp Gordon, Georgia, was very good, very good. And Indian Town Gap I think is where they actually signed us and then we took a train into -- right into the camp. It was funny because when they pulled us out here I am, ex-fireman promoted into there, and finally I'm back on the train. And then from there we went to -- we went out of, I think -- it was either Boston or New York. It was early in the morning, I know, that we went for overseas on the big -- I'm pretty sure it was a big -- the Queen Mary, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Could be.

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: And we had to zig-zag going all the way over. I think there it something around 35 -- I think it was 35,000, or 3,500. Now, I'm not sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Probably 3,500.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that crossing?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: That was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Approximately.

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Oh, I was in Camp Gordon, Georgia, I think, about six months, and then we was going overseas. We went to Liverpool and from Liverpool into North Hampton and from North Hampton we went across the channel. And we got across the channel -- we went on the LST or D or whatever it is that you loaded the troops on there plus you had your Howitzer, because I was in the artillery, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your outfit?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: 254th Field Artillery Battalion. Very good outfit. I liked it very much. But just like I say, I was always treated good. While I was there they sent me to Fort Sill, Oklahoma, for artillery mechanic. I passed that with flying colors. And then when I -- actually I didn't even -- I had basic training. I made Private First class, one stripe. I didn't have to sew that on. Then I got a T5, that's two stripes and a T. I didn't have to put that on. Then when I went to Fort Sill and I come back, then I had T4. They made me sew that on. And then I made Buck Sergeant. I went to Staff Sergeant, from Staff Sergeant, First Sergeant. And then -- actually I might be going a little too fast here but the war -- when the war was over they asked me to reenlist for 90 days and I would have to go to the Pacific and they would make me a warrant officer, and I told them, no, thanks, I will not volunteer now. But I says -- right at the present time, though, I'm not sorry that I didn't because of the life I had, which was the most wonderful anybody had ever had, but otherwise maybe I would have volunteered to go. And just like right now, if they'd have needed me in Iraq, I think if they had said, Come on along, I think I would have if they had told me just to hold a flag.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job most of the time?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, I was even battalion carpenter. I also made sure that the barracks were taken care of good inside and out, and trained other boys doing the same thing. I always had things going pretty smooth for me, though, because everybody helped me. I had no problem. I got along with everybody, that was the main part, but I think that was due mainly due to the training of the three C's because that was run by the army also, and you had to be stricter, you had to dress for retreat, revelry. So actually it was pretty nice, I think. But in the service, I loved it. It just seemed to me I wasn't -- I could stay away from home, I wasn't homesick at any time, but there was a difference now when you got overseas and when you start going through mud and stuff like that and getting shells lying here and that, why, actually you get a little homesick then. And you don't forget to pray, I'll tell you that, because that was the main thing. And I think about the worst part that I really had while I was over there was on Christmas. That was on December, I think, 25th, and I think that was 1944, if I'm not mistaken, and that was in -- we came back from, Erding, Germany -- it's past Holland, we was up into Holland that way. That's where I think they had -- I'm pretty sure it was a 900 gun salute, that was in -- that was after midnight. The sky was lit up just like daylight from the rounds going off. And you could feel the shake of the earth, not that much, but anyhow you could feel the vibration. That was the real thing. But anyway here we was offered in the Stars and Stripes, that was a paper they had for us, they said, We'll have turkey and we'll have stuffing and also you'll get cigarettes because when we went overseas the cigarettes were here. When we were here the cigarettes were over there. So you couldn't buy them. So, anyhow, turned around and here we got caught in a snowstorm between 20 to 24 inches and I think that come down within 24 hours. They had outfits that they called into that -- into the Bulge there. They called them in. I was -- we came through over the Liege Bridge there, and I'll never forget, the Germans lit the sky with flares and airplanes at night and there I was in about the middle. That was the scared part. You could feel that bridge vibrate some because the buzz bombs -- as long as you heard them you was happy. But you couldn't do nothing if you didn't hear them. The only thing was you was waiting for them to land. And if they would land where you could hear them, well, you knew you was safe then. When we got off it was raining, misty, got into the Herken Forrest to set up the Howitzers and that, that was my job, bore sight them in and everything and get them ready for action. And you had a little red light that you had to do that with and at night and miserable, but just like I say, coming back to the snow, we did not have turkey. An infantry outfit was ahead of us and actually they was on the move pretty fast. We was behind them because we was actually supporting them, I suppose, so they was ahead of us. So turn around -- we had the 155 Howitzer, that's a tube recoil, and we got those when we landed into England. We didn't have them in the states. We started out with a 105 Howitzer, and the 105 Howitzer actually the first training we got on that, you would not believe this, I made the Howitzers. That was nothing but a horse and I had two boards that I put nails in so you could slide the trails aside. And the aiming circle was cardboard and numbers on it. We used that, I think, for about two months. That was the training right behind the barracks. Then when we got the 105s, to save ammunition we mounted a .32 caliber, the old 1918, I guess they had -- .32 caliber, it was, the shell, and actually small. It was only about I think five inches is all. And if you had a misfire, that was my job, to take that and handle it with care, you bury it. And then you didn't know if it was going to explode or not. And so then we even had -- then they stopped using those and we mounted .22s, rifles, on the Howitzer, and used them. But the break came finally when we got into England, we got the 155. Those were a very nice gun, tube recoil. They was set on jacks, the others had trails you had to dig in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in England before you went to France?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: I was in England I think about -- oh, we had -- we was down by the Moors there. Anyhow, we was in there I think about two weeks, two weeks, I know that for sure, possibly three, but not any more than that because they took us over. That channel is really rough, it's really rough. And actually we got in there in the morning. I had another good one, the major told me, he says -- in fact, he wasn't a major, he was a colonel. He says to me, he says, Sarge, he says, Take care of all these guns when the troops get off. Well, they waded in water because a tide was coming up and here he says, You be the last one off. Well, I got off, I tell you, but I don't know how I got up to shore. And when I got to shore they was supposed to pick me up. I did not get picked up by anybody and they told us, Do not dive into a ditch or get off the road because if you do they had mines that were wood and mine detectors, I guess, didn't detect them at that time because don't forget it wasn't like the wars that they have now, they can detect so much that it isn't funny. They can stand maybe five yards or better from something and just put their gauges on them and know what's what. But anyhow, so turn around here I was all by myself, it was still early in the morning. I was wet. And I didn't get to my outfit until 1:30 in the afternoon. And they asked me, Where were you? They says, we thought you was lost. And I says, Yes. I asked the colonel, I said, they didn't pick me up, I just bummed a ride here. And he says, You're lucky. But we actually, before they went to -- they had some of the guns left behind, the Howitzers. I actually bore sighted those in. I used the sight off of the White Cliffs of Dover, I won't forget that. So I tell you that was rough. But when I got with the outfit everything was all right. We had smooth sailing then. We had stops, though, a lot of foxholes to dig. Today, I don't know how -- they don't dig them too much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you land in France?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Omaha Beach.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Omaha Beach?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long after D-Day was that?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Oh, gosh, I don't really remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it still in June or was it later?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: It was later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: July or August?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Yeah. Something like that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about the fighting in Normandy? Were they still fighting in Normandy?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, they was actually fighting -- they had stragglers all the way through, you know. Actually to tell you the truth it wasn't -- there was some that was left behind. Actually they didn't even follow the soldiers, they left them behind I think purposely to actually see how many Americans they could get. But just like I always said, you know, they complained -- it isn't all the German soldiers, because you met some that even when we captured them, you talked to them, they did not want to fight. They was forced to fight. I mean they was forced. They did not volunteer like we had chances here to volunteer and train before you even went anyplace. They put them right up on the front line and they put the infantry in front and then they put a group behind them. They could not back up; they had to go forward because if they backed up they would shoot them, that's all. And then we had troubles -- I even have a rifle right here at home that I brought back here as a souvenir that the SS -- they had that school for training for the boys, and they used to actually -- crack shots, they were. They used to take and shoot a soldier just like nothing. See, I think even -- those kids were so good I think they could knock off a soldier at a hundred yards, that's how good some of them were. But then they would just run. You could never catch up with them, maybe you did with some of them but not very many of them. So that was that part. But just like I say, then you had troubles too, if you moved at night they had those tank traps, I fell in one of those. It was cold that time. That was after we got out of the Bulge there. And the only time I think we moved out of the -- out is when the Desert Fox was coming in to chase us back into the ocean, and actually it was cold. We moved, let's see, three miles in 13 hours. I think we didn't eat for two days. Then we got a nice place. Oh, I thought it was heaven. There was a barn there with straw in it and they said, You got to eat before you go. The cooks kind of had, I don't know, a short time before we did. They cooked -- they threw navy beans in I guess ketchup, I think, is what it tasted like to me. Well, the sauce was good but the beans were hard. And I no longer got up there and laid down then they says, You got to move, you go with the forward observers; so we would take and get a place set up. And I used to work where they used to take in the commands and that from the Piper Cubs and those fellows had it rough because they used to have to fly treetops high and they'd come down -- they would land in cornfields that had the mesh, the heavier mesh, and it didn't take no space hardly to stop those. And they would come down and they would take this here tape that we use, duct tape, but it was olive drab, and they would patch the holes and go back up. Those guys used to shake because they had holes through the plane and that. Actually I don't think they was supposed to fire at them, they was supposed to -- that's how we got to find out where they was at. The soldiers -- I mean the German soldiers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Gosh, I can't tell you that. As soon as I hit -- I thought the first date of combat, actually to tell you the truth, was the first day you landed there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. What were you thinking when you landed there?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: To me I was brought up with hunting guns and all that. My dad bought a -- I call it a hog leg, a 12 gauge shotgun, and the first time I shot it at a rabbit I landed about 10 feet back. So the next rabbit that come around my dad says Shoot him, and I says, No. So then he come up to me and says, Why didn't you shoot him right in front of you? And I says, You ought to see my shoulder; it was black and blue. So I actually had gun training, my dad was very good to me, but we never touched a gun at home, or a rifle, never. We always -- he had them right out in the open and the kids never touched them. The shells were never with the gun, though, never.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other stories or memories about the campaign in France before the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, I was looking forward a great deal to Paris. We went into Paris. I don't want to say this the way I saw it, but I can tell you, I was actually disappointed, very disappointed. But war is war so you can't say. But they actually had their bathrooms right in the center of Paris and the one side was like for women, the other side was for men, but it didn't smell too good there. But then you can expect that. But they would even come out -- we'd see them come out -- I don't think it was all people like that, I don't think so. They'd come right out of the pub -- well, it was pubs in English, I don't know what they called them in France anyhow. I called them dives myself. So turn around, they'd come outside and go to the bathroom. I couldn't understand that. But I didn't have too much to do with the French people. But then on the way I met a lot of Polish soldiers, and I'm Polish myself, I can talk Polish, Croatian, and Serbian. So I got along pretty good there. And I think it was in Born [phonetically], Germany -- I'll go up out of France for a minute, and I'll tell you, that was pretty good there. I actually was -- well, I wasn't in charge but they'd take me down there about three times a week, they had a house there, and I would stay in that. That was Polish, Serbian, Croatian, PWs, and that is where I first met General McArthur -- I mean General Eisenhower, and I also met Patton.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You met them?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Yes, I did. I walked right with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Now, the story of that was a nice bigger heart, it fluttered really nice to the rhythm of a good polka because I was so proud. Now, it was raining. Now, Patton would walk in the rain with his boots shined and that -- I'll never forget that head gear he had on. It had I don't know how many layers of varnish on it but it was sharp. And he'd dress tight. I've got an Eisenhower jacket right here in my closet where I'm making this interview from, and I'll tell you, Patton dressed tight. But Eisenhower, not so tight. He was a little sloppier, not as neat. Good, I guess, but he made out pretty good because he was a good general. Turn around and he stayed in the command car, but Patton walked, but I did actually meet them both so I was pretty pleased about that. And I was not in Japan or anyplace there in the Pacific War, but I did meet McArthur, I met him on 172nd and Saint Clare in Cleveland Ohio. I worked with Cleveland Graphite Bronze and he came in with a helicopter, and I actually saw him. And General Rose, he got away with the first bluff, the way I gather, the first bluff he got away. He was a tank general, in a tank battalion or whatever. So anyway, I turn around, the second time he didn't do it; he got killed. But he was another good one. Now, the 82nd Airborne, yeah, I met them. I met them pretty good because they were in the Bulge and they come in with the 105 Howitzers, that's the pack Howitzers. They had small -- I think it was the 32s they used before that, and then they got -- they was a little larger, but I actually took and bore sighted them in but I was not attached to the 82nd Airborne. I was right behind them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was your outfit when the Bulge began?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: I was right -- Liege -- the Herken Forrest, the Herken Forrest, they started going straight through that. But the December thing, I was trying to say, that was bitter cold. Now, when they brought those fellows in -- actually a lot of them didn't have the clothes we had. We had winter clothes on. It was cold, I mean to tell you. And I don't know where they came from, I cannot tell you that for sure, but a lot of them got frostbites -- well, we even had some of our outfit get frostbites and that. But being a farm boy and that, being in the woods all the time, I used to hunt and trap in the wilds and that so actually I made out all right. So I got underneath a pine tree and I took pine limbs and I put them down on the ground, and when I put them on the ground then I put my -- I had two of those pup tents, I put one over that and then the other one I set up and I had my blankets and I'd stay pretty warm. You had canned heat. You could not have fires going, you couldn't even have a cigarette going or nothing like that, but actually -- the only way then, when you couldn't get a cigarette, you used coffee grounds or leaves we used to smoke. Not very good, to tell you the truth. I'm glad I'm still alive. But actually, just like I say, we got out of there. It was a pleasant thing. And then we went to -- I think we was going back up toward the Siegfried Line -- well, I was up to the Siegfried Line and everything there. They was really -- they was just great big pillars, you couldn't get through that darn thing, but we had a lot of problems because you didn't know when you was going into a land mine or one of them anti-personnel mines. They had the S-mines too. The guys used to climb a tree, these men that put in phone wires and that, if they stretched them up on a tree or something like that and they'd jump, they had enough force that when they'd jump they would lose their life or their legs, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was an S-mine exactly, then?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, it was an anti-personnel mine actually. It would take care of a tank and that, but it would detonate if you'd actually jump on it because of your weight and everything, that's what I think, because you don't ignite it. Then one place I didn't have to dig any -- I think that was in Belgium, if I'm not mistaken. We came through Colgne and Munich -- they didn't call it Munich, they called it Munchin, down around the Brightburn [phonetically] Sea there. I'll tell you, the best part was when then I understand that Patton had the right idea -- I still think in my mind he had the right idea, him and Montgomery was always fighting to see who was going to get ahead of who, and in my opinion I'll stick for Patton because I saw him and I met him, so I would stick for him anyhow. He was a fighter because he always said, When you're with me you don't have to dig, he says. With your blood and my guts, he says, we'll get through this and we won't have to dig to do it. But he wanted to go through and take Russia at that time because I understand right now -- it's clear as day -- that we were giving Russia, the planes, ammunition, the food and that because they run out of everything. And if it wasn't for us the Germans would have taken them -- I think it was in Stalingrad -- they would have taken them. But then another smart thing, they wore their regular clothes and the Russians were smart because they wore white clothes and snow was never in color, not unless it was blood, but otherwise no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were with Patton did you ever get a chance to actually talk to him?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: I talked to him because he shook hands with me, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of conversation did you have?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, he asked me, actually, because I was in charge -- they built a beautiful kitchen and brick buildings for these people that was there, they were all pretty good. I mean, I could talk to them and that. And then they have -- in Germany they had brooms but they were made out of twigs, out of trees, some kind of a tree that they used and it was just a wooden handle. That was their broom. Well, we furnished them regular brooms. So he would come around and I guess he must have read something someplace or somebody told Patton, they says, We furnished them brooms. So he says to me, he says, Sarge -- or, Sargent, he says, where are the brooms? And I said, You know something? They use their own. And he says, Yeah, I see that. He says, Where is the ones that they got from us? Well, they take them into town and they sell those and then they keep their own brooms here, but they was pretty good. As a whole things turned out pretty good, because, as I say, I came back. But I did, on that Bulge stuff now that I was saying, we've seen where you'd go into the houses when we was coming in there and holes in the walls and that and there was snow on the ground and with some snow there was already -- the wind blew off and that, we saw soldiers, American soldiers, they threw them out of the upstairs window, they didn't carry them, I know they didn't, they just threw them out. They were on piles. And then the tenth armored, we was up there where they had troubles too because I guess they got them by surprise -- I mean, our tanks did not compare with Germans at that time. I think we could put holes through them, because we saw a lot of them that were actually knocked out completely. But they had their 88th and we had our 105s and up and we did pretty good. But what I wouldn't give in my life today to have the opportunity and the equipment and know-how, the intelligence that the American scientists and these big engineers and that figured out, with the electrical stuff that they got today, I always said, I don't know how many got killed in the last war but I figured at least 700,000 or better, if it was better, I'm sorry, but if we had that equipment that they had in Iraq I think we would have lost maybe at least one third because we was fighting two wars, one in Japan and one in Germany, and we had to split our troops, just about like we got in Germany -- or I mean in Iraq now, we're all over there. We got troops all over as far as that goes, I don't know, a lot of them don't even know America, they're so far away from home and that. And then it's trouble to a soldier to leave that was married. I was one of the smart ones. I had a girlfriend, she wanted to get married the day before I left. I says, No. I told her, I says, I love you but I says, No. She says, Why not? I says, Look, if I lose an arm or a leg, when I come back I don't think you'll have the love for me that I would want from you. But I says, I'll tell you one thing, I'll write to you, which I did. If you do find somebody you love, don't hesitate. I will not feel bad. I did not get a Dear John letter from her, I got one from her sister, Doris could not write the letter. She did get married, and she told me to write the letter to you. So that's the way I got my Dear John. And I came back -- I was going to go see her and just thank her and everything, but I didn't. But to tell you the truth the good Lord was good to me because if I had my life to live over right now from the age of three to being eighty, I would want nothing changed, I would live it the same way, have the same jobs I had, and I said in my life I had at least maybe 30 or 40 jobs. I loved some of them, some of them I didn't. If I didn't like a job I could get off of it, I could get the work I wanted, I never had no trouble. And I would also want to marry the same woman the Lord let me have because I knew her when she was six and we got married in 1947 and we lived together for 55 years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Had plenty of buddies. You had to make buddies. You needed friends. If you got an enemy that's the one you watched but you had -- that way you would have two enemies, the one in front of you and the one in back. Got along pretty good. Never had a problem getting along. Never had arguments with the guys, that way you always got along good. When I was First Sergeant I never had trouble with my men. In fact, one time the captain come in, he says, Sergeant, he says, Don't you want to talk to so and so about this and that? And I says, I can talk to him if you want me to. He says I wish you would. Everything was straightened out. I never had no trouble. And I think it's wonderful when you have that. You might get one and think or say something but then he'll come back and apologize. And I always say apologize, if it's from the heart, take it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever have a chance to do anything for entertainment or fun with your buddies?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Not during a time of war. Actually, the funniest part, I went into basic training -- I'll go back that far now again. I had the railroad pass so I got the railroad pass, six days they gave me, three days at home, three days traveling time. So I didn't have much time at home and, you know, shipped overseas. Now -- but I was just, like I say, fortunate. Over there now actually they come up to me and they says, Sarge -- they did call me sarge -- so I turn around and they says, How would you like to take and go wherever you want, he says, on a 14 day pass. Well, I actually figured since I'm Polish to try to get to Poland. Well, at that time they tried to arrange it but some difficulties there so what would your next bet be, and I went to Switzerland. Beautiful country. Beautiful. People were good because a lot of them could talk American and then, of course, you had -- the foreign languages I knew, they had them there too. But the people were very nice there and they treated you good. The hotels and everything was clean and nice. We stayed in hotels and they had our food but they still had some rationing on stuff there too, like -- well, you could buy -- if you wanted alcohol and that you could buy that, there was plenty of that there, but I mean bread and stuff like that. So I wanted -- they had the same thing as we had, I think, your coupons or something and that you could get it. So I came into this bakery, it smelled so good. I was in it alone, maybe it's a good thing, then they told me, well, they could take me in the back room, and they gave me some bread, cheese, and stuff like that. It was very good. But I just had my fill. I didn't ask for more than they gave me and I appreciated what they gave me. But in Germany I used to trade that P&G or Naptha soap, whatever it is with lye in it, they used to wash my clothes, and I used to trade them for big loaves of bread, that was heavy rye bread, they made it in these open ovens, and very good, and you could carry that with you about four or five days. So you had to be a little conniver now and then, but they didn't bother you if you did that. They was pretty good. And if I come to a place and I saw a garden dug up in spots, well, I used to dig myself. That's where I used to find bacon wrapped up in I think it was canvas and they had wax on it and they would put it in the ground and they would cover it up. Of course when we went through, then, the ones that would come back why they had something to eat but a lot of times they was short because I had a lot of that. But I don't know, I always had it pretty good. Or sometimes -- and I hate to say this -- but I'd pour out that five gallon of water out of that darned container and I'd fill it up with a nice five gallons of wine. We would have a nip now and then, or warm it up, very good for you. But we didn't get drunk on it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Yes, but then actually our outfit was pretty fortunate. We lost a few in the battalion but as a rule we come out of it pretty good, I'd say, you know. We were followers. We went through but we was always moving, always moving. Those that sit still, they'd find out you're there I think are the ones that would get hurt the most because the artillery would get them, or you know, they had planes too. But they ever never computed to us anyhow, I don't care how much training you had. The only ones you had to watch was the SS and that, and, like I say, the boys that had rifles. But actually I still say even going through the war, I still wouldn't trade my life. I wouldn't want to go through it again as far as that goes because it was no fun, I mean, a big problem for parents at home, always waiting from day-to-day to hear something good and sometimes our letters weren't coming in as often as they should and now I understand if the girl that I was going with, she'd have saved all those letters, those one page letters they used to give us to mail, why today to e-mail them, my gosh they're buying those and here I wrote a lot of letters and I don't know, I'll have to see if I can get a hold of her, maybe her and I can go into business. But we had -- just like I say, you can't be a loner, you can't be a loner. You have to get along or else you're in trouble. You've got to have friends.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was your outfit attached to the Third Army the whole time?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Third Army and Ninth Army, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you come home?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: I come home in '46.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you part of the Army of Occupation for a while in Europe?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: No, they started it when I was getting ready to come home. But I would have stayed there. (END OF SIDE ONE, CD ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, CD ONE.) MR. MATYJASIK: Because occupation, you might as well say it's just a vacation, you know, nothing -- this wasn't like in Iraq, they're still killing our men and I don't know -- I think they're rushing this here a little too fast. I think they should have kept more troops there regardless of what they said. We liberated them, we helped them, and what they should realize now, you can't trust nobody there. And even if it's a kid, he can pick up a gun anyplace, or a rifle or whatever. And I don't think it's right but you can't stay there forever because, just like I say, we still got men in Germany yet from the first war. Not the same ones as in the second world war, but we still got them there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: And I don't know. I don't know if we got any in France, I don't like what they're doing, but that besides the point. The English, they was pretty good to us when we was there but we helped them out because we come in when they was in trouble and I am certainly glad that Mr. Blair or whatever rank or -- I don't know what you would call him by, but anyhow he did a good job to join Bush on that because actually it did -- it was fast. It was fast. It was amazing how fast. I says, ours would have been, my gosh, I think -- I don't think we'd have lasted -- maybe ours would have lasted at least a year but we had two fronts, but we wouldn't have had the casualties we had, we would have never had that. That was good the way this worked, but I just hope it stops right now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during World War II does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Chester Michael Matyjasik
sp.p: Well, I never -- I thought maybe they'd get together and people would be a lot different, and I don't know, it just don't seem like -- I always say as long as people live as humans, if there's two men in this country they'll still have a fight between one another, or no different if it was two ladies because it was in the service -- I compared this to service -- that if it was two ladies one would want more than the other and there was only two of them left they would still have a fight to see who was the greatest or whatever, I don't know. But my point is right now love everybody because it doesn't make any difference what color they are. I say, just make sure that you can live from day-to-day, get up in the morning and, like I say, Good morning, Lord, I've got another day. What I make of it is mine. You gave it to me to start with, if you want to finish it back, do what you want to do. So that's why I say anyplace I go they call me Mr. Lucky. And, I don't know, I might have a wrong philosophy in life and they tell me -- why, I set up my flags in the yard every Memorial Day for the last 48 years at least. I started out with 13 flags, that's five small ones, I still got them, and the 48 star that I started with, the three by five, is out of color now, it's not the color it should be, but I still hang it up. And that one I'm going to take with me when I leave this country forever and go wherever I'm supposed to go. That will be at the foot of my casket because I honor the flag. I love the flags, I've got them in my house, I've got them outside, and I can mention I had 300 or a little better than 300 for Memorial Day. I got good coverage from different stations on televisions, it was 19, and also Channel 3, and then they said they had me on Channel 8. And then I saw another segment there they had me in with the events that was going around in town and my picture was in on that. And then they had me in the Plain Dealer also. And I had so many people here and children that took at least camera shots, they took -- they emptied their cameras here. But people enjoyed it, they all talked to me. Now I go to the score, I hear the kids saying, Flagman is here. So it makes me feed good, though. And just like I say, don't underestimate the United States, love it, and just like they say, if you don't, leave it, and don't come back if you don't love it. Don't hurt it because it can hurt you. You'll be sorry one of these days because everybody is trying to, say, take a little piece of us, and it don't pay. Join us, you can have the whole thing from the heart on. That's my version of living life in peace and I'm always happy. I help now the seniors that are older than myself, and I do not charge them. They thank me and it makes me feel good also. A lot of friends, wherever I go, whatever I do. So how's that?
